docs.title: dev-aliases
docs.text:
I got tired of typing terraform apply --auto-approve and git log --oneline a hundred times a day, so I made this.

It's a simple installer that sets up short aliases for Terraform and Git on Windows — works in both CMD and PowerShell.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text:
Tool Count Aliases Terraform 10 tf tfi tfp tfa tfd tfv tff tfo tfs tfws Git 18 g gs ga gc gp gl gb gco gd glog gst gstp grs grss gm grb grt gcl

Docker and kubectl aliases are coming — feel free to contribute!

docs.title: Before vs after
docs.text:
Before: 

terraform apply --auto-approve
git log --oneline
git restore --staged .

After: 

tfa
glog
grss .

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Installation — takes less than a minute
  • Alias Reference — full list with examples
  • Contributing — add your own aliases

docs.title: Alias Reference
docs.text: Full list of all aliases with what they do and some common workflows I use daily.

docs.title: Terraform
docs.text: Alias Command What it does tf terraform base terraform command tfi terraform init initialize directory, download providers tfp terraform plan preview what's going to change tfa terraform apply --auto-approve apply without the yes/no prompt tfd terraform destroy --auto-approve destroy everything without prompt tfv terraform validate check if config files have errors tff terraform fmt auto-format all .tf files tfo terraform output show output values from state tfs terraform show inspect current state tfws terraform workspace manage workspaces

docs.title: How I use these day to day
docs.text:
# starting a new project
tfi
tfv
tfp
tfa

# check what's deployed
tfs
tfo

# switching workspaces
tfws list
tfws select staging

# tearing down
tfd

docs.title: Git
docs.text: Alias Command What it does g git base git command gs git status see what's changed ga git add stage files gc git commit commit staged changes gp git push push to remote gl git pull pull latest from remote gb git branch list or manage branches gco git checkout switch branches or restore files gd git diff see unstaged changes glog git log --oneline compact commit history gst git stash stash current changes gstp git stash pop bring back stashed changes grs git restore discard changes in a file grss git restore --staged unstage a file gm git merge merge a branch grb git rebase rebase onto another branch grt git remote -v see configured remotes gcl git clone clone a repo

docs.title: My usual workflows
docs.text:
# everyday commit
gs
ga .
gc -m "feat: something"
gp

# working on a feature branch
gb my-feature
gco my-feature
# ... do work ...
ga .
gc -m "feat: done"
gp

# need to switch context quickly
gst                   # stash current work
gco main
gl
gco my-feature
gstp                  # get stashed work back

# made a mistake
grs file.txt          # throw away changes in a file
grss file.txt         # unstage something
glog                  # check history

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: If you want to add aliases for Docker, kubectl, AWS CLI or anything else — go for it. Here's how.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Fork the repo, clone it, create a branch:

gcl https://github.com/your-username/install-dev-aliases.git
gco -b feat/add-docker-aliases

docs.title: Adding a new tool
docs.text: You need to touch three places:

docs.title: 1. scripts/install.cmd
docs.text:
Add a block under the Creating CMD aliases section:

:: ---------- Docker ----------
(echo @echo off & echo docker %%*)           > "%ALIAS_DIR%\d.cmd"
(echo @echo off & echo docker ps %%*)        > "%ALIAS_DIR%\dps.cmd"
(echo @echo off & echo docker logs -f %%*)   > "%ALIAS_DIR%\dlogs.cmd"

docs.title: 2. scripts/install.ps1
docs.text:
Add to the $cmdAliases hashtable:

"d.cmd"     = "docker %*"
"dps.cmd"   = "docker ps %*"
"dlogs.cmd" = "docker logs -f %*"

And add the matching functions to the $block here-string:

# Docker
function d       { docker @args }
function dps     { docker ps @args }
function dlogs   { docker logs -f @args }

docs.title: 3. Docs
docs.text:
• Add a table in docs/aliases-reference.md
  • Update the summary table in docs/index.md
  • Update README.md

docs.title: Submitting
docs.text:
ga .
gc -m "feat: add Docker aliases"
gp origin feat/add-docker-aliases

Open a PR with a short description of what you added and why it's useful.

docs.title: A few things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• Keep alias names short — 2 to 5 characters
  • Only add commands you'd actually use in real DevOps work
  • Make sure it doesn't clash with an existing system command
  • Test it in both CMD and PowerShell before submitting

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Just pick whichever script matches your shell and run it. Both do the exact same thing.

docs.title: What it sets up
docs.text:
• .cmd wrapper files in %USERPROFILE%\bin so aliases work in CMD
  • PowerShell functions added to your $PROFILE so aliases work in PS too
  • %USERPROFILE%\bin added to your User PATH automatically
  • Re-running the script is safe — it always updates to the latest aliases

docs.title: CMD
docs.text:
Double-click the file or run it from any terminal:

Download install.cmd

scripts\install.cmd

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
If you haven't done this before, you need to allow local scripts first:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned

Then run the installer:

Download install.ps1

.\scripts\install.ps1

Restart your terminal after running the script — otherwise the aliases won't be available yet.

docs.title: Quick check
docs.text:
After restarting, try these to confirm everything works:

tf --version    # runs: terraform --version
gs              # runs: git status
glog            # runs: git log --oneline

docs.title: Manual Setup (no script)
docs.text: If you'd rather do it yourself, here's exactly what the script does step by step.

docs.title: 1. Create the alias directory
docs.text: mkdir %USERPROFILE%\bin

docs.title: 2. Create CMD alias files
docs.text:
For each alias, create a .cmd file in %USERPROFILE%\bin. For example:

echo @echo off > %USERPROFILE%\bin\tf.cmd
echo terraform %%* >> %USERPROFILE%\bin\tf.cmd

echo @echo off > %USERPROFILE%\bin\tfi.cmd
echo terraform init %%* >> %USERPROFILE%\bin\tfi.cmd

Repeat for each alias you want. See the full list in Alias Reference.

docs.title: 3. Add to PATH
docs.text:
Open Start → Edit environment variables for your account → find Path → click Edit → add %USERPROFILE%\bin.

Or run this in PowerShell:

$path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User')
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', $path + ';' + "$HOME\bin", 'User')

docs.title: 4. Add PowerShell aliases
docs.text:
Open your PowerShell profile:

notepad $PROFILE

If the file doesn't exist yet:

New-Item -ItemType File -Path $PROFILE -Force

Add these functions at the bottom:

# Terraform
function tf      { terraform @args }
function tfi     { terraform init @args }
function tfp     { terraform plan @args }
function tfa     { terraform apply --auto-approve @args }
function tfd     { terraform destroy --auto-approve @args }
function tfv     { terraform validate @args }
function tff     { terraform fmt @args }
function tfo     { terraform output @args }
function tfs     { terraform show @args }
function tfws    { terraform workspace @args }

# Git
function g       { git @args }
function gs      { git status @args }
function ga      { git add @args }
function gc      { git commit @args }
function gp      { git push @args }
function gl      { git pull @args }
function gb      { git branch @args }
function gco     { git checkout @args }
function gd      { git diff @args }
function glog    { git log --oneline @args }
function gst     { git stash @args }
function gstp    { git stash pop @args }
function grs     { git restore @args }
function grss    { git restore --staged @args }
function gm      { git merge @args }
function grb     { git rebase @args }
function grt     { git remote -v @args }
function gcl     { git clone @args }

Save and restart your terminal.

docs.title: Using TF_DATA_DIR to Save Disk Space
docs.text: By default, Terraform creates a .terraform folder inside each project. This folder contains provider binaries (like aws.exe ~800MB), which means every project ends up with its own duplicate copy — quickly consuming disk space.

docs.title: The TF_DATA_DIR Trick
docs.text:
Terraform supports an environment variable called TF_DATA_DIR that lets you override where the .terraform working directory is stored.

Example (Windows PowerShell): 

setx TF_DATA_DIR "C:\terraform-shared"

Once set, all your projects will use C:\terraform-shared as their .terraform folder instead of creating one locally. Providers download once and get reused across every project.

docs.title: Before vs After
docs.text:
Before — every project downloads its own copy: 

C:\projects\
├── project-a\
│   └── .terraform\        # ~800MB aws.exe
├── project-b\
│   └── .terraform\        # ~800MB aws.exe (duplicate)
└── project-c\
    └── .terraform\        # ~800MB aws.exe (duplicate)

After — one shared copy for all projects: 

C:\terraform-shared\       # ~800MB aws.exe (shared)

C:\projects\
├── project-a\             # no .terraform folder
├── project-b\             # no .terraform folder
└── project-c\             # no .terraform folder

docs.title: How to Set It Up
docs.text:
Run one of these scripts — they create the shared directory and set TF_DATA_DIR permanently.

CMD:

Download setup-terraform-cache.cmd

scripts\setup-terraform-cache.cmd

PowerShell:

Download setup-terraform-cache.ps1

.\scripts\setup-terraform-cache.ps1

Both scripts are safe to run multiple times — they skip steps that are already done.

docs.title: What Gets Created
docs.text:
C:\terraform-shared — single shared directory used by all projects

User environment variable: 

TF_DATA_DIR=C:\terraform-shared

Restart your terminal after running, then do terraform init in any project — providers will be stored in C:\terraform-shared and reused across all your projects from that point on.

docs.title: Manual Setup (no script)
docs.text: If you'd rather do it yourself, here are the exact steps.

docs.title: 1. Create the shared directory
docs.text: mkdir C:\terraform-shared

docs.title: 2. Set TF_DATA_DIR permanently
docs.text:
CMD: 

setx TF_DATA_DIR "C:\terraform-shared"

PowerShell: 

[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('TF_DATA_DIR', 'C:\terraform-shared', 'User')

Or via GUI: Start → Edit environment variables for your account → New → set name TF_DATA_DIR and value C:\terraform-shared.

docs.title: 3. Restart your terminal
docs.text: Then run terraform init in any project — it will use C:\terraform-shared from now on.
